To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the Facebook cases in Germany and Italy show that the EU competition and consumer law regimes have similar objectives, rules and remedies to tackle anticompetitive and anticonsumer practices; (b) the Facebook cases also show the limits of these legal regimes in addressing market failures in the digital economy, and that a comprehensive regulatory approach is necessary; and (c) the Facebook cases are also a good illustration of the regulatory competition between the EU competition and the consumer law regimes.
competition, consumer and privacy law have different objectives, rules and remedies.

EU competition, consumer, and data protection law can be applied to digital markets, and they have been applied to digital markets in the past, and that the application of competition and data protection law to digital markets is more likely to lead to a positive outcome for consumers than the application of consumer law.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how competition law can be used to protect consumers in digital markets, and whether competition law is the best tool to achieve this objective.
the question of how to regulate the digital economy.
the following question: which regulatory regime is best equipped to address the market failures arising from the use of personal data in digital markets?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EU regulatory framework is still fragmented.
competition law is not the right instrument to regulate digital platforms and their data-driven business models.
the EU's current competition, consumer and privacy laws are inadequate to regulate digital markets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
competition law is ill-suited to address these failures.
the current legal framework is not able to effectively address the market failures in the digital economy.
the current regulatory framework is not able to adequately address these problems, and that a more comprehensive reform of competition law is needed.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the current regulatory framework in Europe is not adequate to tackle the problems of the digital economy and that the interaction between the different EU regulatory regimes is far from being satisfactory.
competition, consumer, and data protection law are not mutually exclusive.

, while competition law is well equipped to address exploitative abuses of dominance involving digital platforms, it is not the best suited tool to tackle the privacy-related issues that are at the heart of these cases.
